items.title: Advantages of Sampling

sections.normalized_html: Contrary to sampling, a census is a study in which data is collected from every member of the population. For example, if a school lunch survey included every student in the school, it would be a census.
sections.readable_text: Contrary to sampling, a census is a study in which data is collected from every member of the population. For example, if a school lunch survey included every student in the school, it would be a census.

sections.normalized_html: Sampling has several advantages over a census:
sections.readable_text: Sampling has several advantages over a census:

sections.normalized_html:
• Sampling is cheaper and faster

    Conducting a census can be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, especially for large populations. A sample provides useful information much more quickly and at a lower cost.
sections.readable_text:
- Sampling is cheaper and faster

Conducting a census can be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, especially for large populations. A sample provides useful information much more quickly and at a lower cost.

sections.normalized_html:
• Sample data is more readily available

    When a population is very large or widely dispersed, gathering information from every unit is impractical.

    For example, to study the average age of deer in a certain county, it would be nearly impossible to locate every deer. By sampling a smaller group, we can still make reliable estimates.

- Sample data is more readily available

For example, to study the average age of deer in a certain county, it would be nearly impossible to locate every deer. By sampling a smaller group, we can still make reliable estimates.

sections.normalized_html:
• Sampling is necessary when testing causes destruction

    Some studies require destroying the sampling units being tested.

    For example, to determine the average lifetime of a battery, testing every battery in a population would render them all useless. By sampling, we can estimate the average lifetime while preserving most of the population.

items.title: Disadvantages of Sampling

sections.normalized_html: Because a sample represents only part of the population, the way it is chosen matters. If the selection process is flawed, the sample may be biased.
sections.readable_text: Because a sample represents only part of the population, the way it is chosen matters. If the selection process is flawed, the sample may be biased.

sections.normalized_html: For example, if a survey about school lunches only included girls, the results may not represent the opinions of the entire student body.
sections.readable_text: For example, if a survey about school lunches only included girls, the results may not represent the opinions of the entire student body.

sections.normalized_html: Sampling, therefore, has several disadvantages over a census.
sections.readable_text: Sampling, therefore, has several disadvantages over a census.

sections.normalized_html:
• Samples can be biased

    If the sampling method is poorly designed or executed, the results may not accurately represent the population.

  • Samples show natural variation

    There will always be some variation between any two samples due to differences among the sampling units that make them up.

  • Sampling error is unavoidable

    Because a sample is only a subset of the population, estimates from a sample may differ from the true population values.

  • Rare characteristics may be missed

    Certain uncommon features may not appear in a sample if the sample size is too small or if the selection method is inadequate.

Certain uncommon features may not appear in a sample if the sample size is too small or if the selection method is inadequate.

items.title: Identifying Advantages of Samples

sections.normalized_html: A meteorological research institute wants to estimate the average annual rainfall in remote villages across a large desert region. Why might the institute choose to use a sample instead of conducting a census?
sections.readable_text: A meteorological research institute wants to estimate the average annual rainfall in remote villages across a large desert region. Why might the institute choose to use a sample instead of conducting a census?

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Advantages of sampling:

  • Sampling is generally cheaper and faster than taking a census.

  • Sample data is more readily available, especially when the population is large or widely dispersed.

  • Sampling is useful when testing items leads to their destruction (e.g., testing for the average lifetime of a battery).

  • Sampling can allow more intensive study of each unit (e.g., collecting more detailed measurements than would be feasible in a census).

In this case, traveling to every remote village in the desert to record rainfall data would be extremely time-consuming, costly, and logistically challenging. By selecting a representative sample of villages from different parts of the region, the institute can still estimate the average rainfall without needing to visit every single village.

Sampling is more practical for gathering data when the population is widely dispersed.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In statistics, a population is the complete set of individuals or objects about which information is sought.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- If we want to determine the voting intentions in an upcoming U.S. presidential election, the population would consist of all eligible voters in the United States.
- If a scientist wants to study the average sugar content in oranges grown in Spain during a particular growing season, the population would be every orange produced in Spain during that season.

Content:
These examples show that studying every element of a population is often impractical — it may be too costly, too time-consuming, or simply impossible. Instead, we typically gather information from a smaller group that's representative of the whole population. This smaller subset is called a sample.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/73836f0700c86cfb75d846867e6318f2]

Content:
When conducting a sample, the sampling units are the individual elements of a population from which observations are taken and could be selected in a sample.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- If we want to determine the voting intentions of the population in an upcoming U.S. presidential election, the sampling units are the individual eligible voters.
- If we want to determine the average sugar content in oranges grown in Spain during a particular growing season, the sampling units are the individual oranges.

Content:
An investigation that's carried out using a sample is called a survey.

---

Item 2 — Example: Identifying Sampling Units

Example Prompt:
A transportation agency is studying car ownership in a suburban neighborhood. The neighborhood has [MATH: 1{,}500] households. Surveyors randomly select [MATH: 75] households and record the number of cars owned by each household.

What are the sampling units in this study?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The sampling units are the individual elements of a population from which observations are taken and could be selected in a sample.

In this case, the sampling units are the individual households in the suburban neighborhood. Each household is the basic unit selected for the sample, and the number of cars is recorded for each one. Although the data involve the people in the households, the selection is at the household level.

---

Item 3 — Question 1

Prompt:
A wildlife biologist is studying a population of [MATH: 240] sea turtles in a coastal bay. She randomly selects a group of turtles from the population and records whether each turtle has barnacles on its shell.

What are the sampling units in this study?

Choices:
a. All sea turtles in the coastal bay
b. Barnacles on the turtles’ shells
c. Individual sea turtles in the coastal bay
d. Groups of sea turtles in the coastal bay
e. The entire population of sea turtles worldwide

---

Item 4 — Question 2

Prompt:
An environmental agency is studying plant diversity in a large grassland. The grassland is divided into [MATH: 500] square plots, each measuring [MATH: 10 × 10] meters. Researchers randomly select [MATH: 50] plots and record the number of different plant species growing in each plot.

What are the sampling units in this study?

Choices:
a. All plants in the grassland
b. Groups of plants of the same species
c. Individual plots in the grassland
d. Individual plants in the grassland
e. The entire grassland

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Sampling Frames

Content:
A sampling frame is the list or set of sampling units from which a sample is drawn.

Content:
For example:

Content:
- If we want to determine the voting intentions of the population in an upcoming U.S. presidential election, the sampling frame is a list containing all eligible voters.
- If a scientist wants to estimate the average sugar content in oranges grown in Spain during a particular season, the sampling frame might be a catalog or registry of all orchards in Spain along with their harvest inventories.

Content:
Typically, the sample is chosen from the sampling frame at random to fairly represent the population. We'll discuss this in more detail shortly.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/7b8fc76f4e81e2983f6c41ae8db9beed]

---

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Sampling Frames

Example Prompt:
A university IT department wants to estimate the proportion of computers on campus running the latest operating system. They obtain a complete list of the [MATH: 3{,}200] device inventory numbers from the campus asset database and randomly select [MATH: 150] computers to check.

What is the sampling frame in this study?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
A sampling frame is the list or set of sampling units from which a sample is drawn.

In this case, the sampling frame is the list of all [MATH: 3{,}200] device inventory numbers obtained from the campus asset database. This is the set of all possible computers (the sampling units) that could be selected for the check.

---

A university health center wants to estimate the proportion of dorm rooms that have a working carbon monoxide detector. They obtain a complete list of the [MATH: 4,500] dorm room numbers from the housing office and randomly select [MATH: 200] rooms to inspect.

What is the sampling frame in this study?

Choices:
a. The [MATH: 200] dorm rooms selected for inspection
b. All houses in the town
c. All students enrolled at the university
d. The list of all [MATH: 4,500] dorm room numbers

What is the sampling frame in this study?

Choices:

Item 9 — Tutorial: Advantages of Sampling

Content:
Contrary to sampling, a census is a study in which data is collected from every member of the population. For example, if a school lunch survey included every student in the school, it would be a census.

Content:
Sampling has several advantages over a census:

Content:
- Sampling is cheaper and faster

Conducting a census can be prohibitively expensive and time-consuming, especially for large populations. A sample provides useful information much more quickly and at a lower cost.

Content:
- Sample data is more readily available

When a population is very large or widely dispersed, gathering information from every unit is impractical.

For example, to study the average age of deer in a certain county, it would be nearly impossible to locate every deer. By sampling a smaller group, we can still make reliable estimates.

Content:
- Sampling is necessary when testing causes destruction

Some studies require destroying the sampling units being tested.

For example, to determine the average lifetime of a battery, testing every battery in a population would render them all useless. By sampling, we can estimate the average lifetime while preserving most of the population.

Content:
- Sampling allows for more intensive study of each unit

Because fewer units are studied, researchers can afford to collect more detailed or higher-quality measurements than would be feasible in a census.

---

Item 10 — Tutorial: Disadvantages of Sampling

Content:
Because a sample represents only part of the population, the way it is chosen matters. If the selection process is flawed, the sample may be biased.

Content:
For example, if a survey about school lunches only included girls, the results may not represent the opinions of the entire student body.

Content:
Sampling, therefore, has several disadvantages over a census.

Content:
- Samples can be biased

If the sampling method is poorly designed or executed, the results may not accurately represent the population.
- Samples show natural variation

There will always be some variation between any two samples due to differences among the sampling units that make them up.
- Sampling error is unavoidable

Because a sample is only a subset of the population, estimates from a sample may differ from the true population values.
- Rare characteristics may be missed

Certain uncommon features may not appear in a sample if the sample size is too small or if the selection method is inadequate.

Content:
To reduce these problems, we often conduct a random sample, where each element of the population has an equal chance of being chosen. We will explore the details of bias and random sampling in future lessons.

---

Item 11 — Example: Identifying Advantages of Samples

Example Prompt:
A meteorological research institute wants to estimate the average annual rainfall in remote villages across a large desert region. Why might the institute choose to use a sample instead of conducting a census?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Advantages of sampling:

- Sampling is generally cheaper and faster than taking a census.
- Sample data is more readily available, especially when the population is large or widely dispersed.
- Sampling is useful when testing items leads to their destruction (e.g., testing for the average lifetime of a battery).
- Sampling can allow more intensive study of each unit (e.g., collecting more detailed measurements than would be feasible in a census).

In this case, traveling to every remote village in the desert to record rainfall data would be extremely time-consuming, costly, and logistically challenging. By selecting a representative sample of villages from different parts of the region, the institute can still estimate the average rainfall without needing to visit every single village.

Sampling is more practical for gathering data when the population is widely dispersed.

---
